PLANT GUIDE · STAPELIA GRANDIFLORA

Stapelia grandiflora

Stapelia grandiflora Masson — carrion flower · starfish flower · giant toad plant

One of the most dramatic succulents you can grow indoors, famous for two things: huge, star-shaped flowers of deep maroon velvet — and the smell that comes with them, a perfume of carrion brewed for blowflies. It is not a cactus at all, but a milkweed relative from the dry Karoo of South Africa: soft, spineless, four-angled stems doing the work of leaves, and a balloon bud that swells for days before it splits into the great dark star.

🔍 Anatomy — What It Looks Like

The stems come first: thick, four-angled, and green, growing upright in clumps 6 to 12 inches tall. They look a bit like a cactus — but they are soft and spineless, their angles lined with small teeth that never prick. The stems are the whole plant: there are no true leaves to speak of, only these velvet columns storing water against the drought.

The flowers are the real show. Each bloom runs 5 to 8 inches across, flat and star-shaped, with five pointed, velvety petals in deep maroon to purple-brown, ribbed with fine transverse wrinkles, fringed with long hairs, and marked with lighter yellowish tracery toward the center. Against the giant cousin, S. gigantea — cream-yellow stars lined in red, up to twice the size — grandiflora is told by its dark uniform color and by its bud: a plump balloon, rounded where the segments meet, where gigantea's comes to a point.

Bloom time is mostly late summer into fall, the flowers opening one after another from the base of the younger stems — but a happy plant in bright light can bloom off and on through the warm months. Each flower lasts several days.

🌿 The names: Stapelia honors Johannes Bodaeus van Stapel, the Dutch physician who wrote on Theophrastus in the 1600s; grandiflora is plain Latin for “large-flowered.” The species was described in 1797 by Francis Masson — Kew Gardens’ first plant hunter, sent to the Cape of Good Hope by Sir Joseph Banks — and his painted portrait of it appears below, in the species section.

🪰 Why It Smells

This flower is pollinated by flies, not bees — and it works hard to deserve them. It mimics rotting meat in both looks and scent: the dark red-brown of old flesh, a surface wrinkled and haired like hide, and a carrion odor that runs from faint to strong. A blowfly reads all of it as dinner and a nursery. It lands, it wanders the flower’s heart, and it leaves with the plant’s pollen clipped to it in tiny saddlebags — the milkweed family’s machinery, carried on a fly.

The deception is thorough. The long hairs stir in moving air like fur on something freshly dead; fooled females may even lay their eggs in the flower’s center, where the hatchlings find no food at all. The plant pays nothing for its pollination — the whole fee is a lie, told in color, texture, and smell.

Indoors, the smell is usually noticeable only if you get close to an open bloom. Outside on a porch, you might notice it more on a warm day, when the perfume carries.

🌿 House rule: it is not a plant for right next to the dinner table when it is in bloom. In flower, it earns a spot on the porch — all of the spectacle, none of the aroma at arm’s length.

🎛️ Conditions — Measured

A desert rhythm, kept indoors: fierce light, one thorough drink, then drought until the next. In West Virginia that makes it a houseplant with a summer holiday — out on the porch in morning sun once nights are warm, and back on a bright sill long before the first frost. It is hardy outdoors only in Zones 9–11; here, the windowsill is its Karoo.

📋 The Care Card

LightBright light, with some direct morning sun. Too little light means no flowers — the commonest disappointment with this plant. Too much harsh afternoon sun can sunburn the stems, so give it the morning and shade the blaze.
SoilVery well-draining cactus / succulent mix — gritty, lean, and fast through the pot. It hates wet feet, and more of these plants die of kindness in rich, soggy soil than of anything else.
WaterWater thoroughly, then let it dry out completely before watering again. In winter, water very sparingly — just enough to keep the stems from shriveling. Cold, wet soil is the one combination it cannot forgive.
TemperatureIt loves warmth: 65–85°F in the growing season. Keep it above 50°F in winter — it is not frost-hardy, and a single cold night on a wet root ball can end it.
PotA shallow pot with drainage holes works best, since the roots are shallow. It likes to be a bit root-bound — that snugness is part of what persuades it to bloom — so repot only every two or three years.
FeedingA light cactus fertilizer once a month in spring and summer is plenty. Nothing in winter, while the plant rests.

✂️ Propagation — Snap, Callus, Root

  1. Snap off a stem. The stems separate willingly at their joints — one healthy stem, snapped clean, is the whole harvest.
  2. Let the cut end callus over. Lay the cutting aside in open air for 2–3 days while the cut dries and seals.
  3. Lay it on dry soil. Set the callused stem on the surface of dry cactus mix. No burying, no watering yet.
  4. Wait for roots. It will root in a few weeks. Once it stands on its own roots, water it on the parent’s rhythm.
🌿 Why the callus matters: a fresh-cut stem set straight onto damp soil rots before it can root. The dry seal is the whole trick — and the same patience rescues a stem gone mushy at the base, below.

🩺 Common Problems

RotThe great killer — almost always from overwatering, or cold, wet soil. If a stem turns mushy and brown at the base, cut off the healthy part above the rot, callus it, and re-root it as a cutting.
No flowersUsually not enough light, or the plant is too young. It needs to be a bit root-bound and sun-stressed to bloom well — comfort makes stems, light makes stars.
MealybugsThe resident pest of succulents. Check the joints where the stems meet for white cottony clusters, and dab them with rubbing alcohol on a cotton swab.
✅

Safe around animals. Stapelia grandiflora is not known to be toxic to people, cats, or dogs. The flower’s only offense is its perfume — admire it up close, briefly, and let the flies have the rest.

🏜️ The Species Beyond the Pot

In the wild it grows scattered through the Great Karoo and the Eastern Cape, often in the shade of shrubs — one of the best-recorded of all South African stapeliads, and, with its giant cousin, among the most widely grown in the world. The seed end of the story asks patience: a pollinated flower folds into twin horns that can take a full year to ripen, then split to loose flat seeds on silky parachutes, away on the wind like its milkweed kin.
